issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: The trigger profile mixes tactile/startle-type cues and driving-with-others cues that could fit war-zone trauma, but 'being looked at sexually' points toward a sexual-threat trauma context that is not supported elsewhere in memory, threat, or appraisal items. This specific trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The dominant threat items describe generalized vigilance and fear of interpersonal attack. In combination with the sexual-objectification trigger, this pulls the profile toward an interpersonal/sexual trauma formulation, whereas the memory and appraisal items do not contain corresponding themes. This creates cross-node incoherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is not impossible, but in this profile it lacks a clear link to the other selected items. The rest of the appraisals center on unfairness, shame, and inability to trust oneself; without any role-related trauma content in memory, triggers, or threat, this item feels weakly anchored and clinically mismatched relative to the otherwise war-zone/interpersonal-danger presentation.

vignette:
Kealani had been a veterinarian for twenty years, a profession she chose for its quiet certainties and the gentle logic of healing. That logic was shattered eight months ago. Volunteering with an animal rescue NGO during a regional conflict, she was helping evacuate a shelter in a repurposed delivery van. She remembers the frantic energy, the smell of dust and fear, the press of other aid workers and crated animals. The memory of the event itself does not exist as a coherent story, but as a series of sharp, disconnected pieces: the sudden, deafening roar of the roadside bomb, the violent lurch of the van, the feeling of being thrown hard against the metal siding. A man’s hand grabbed her arm in the darkness, a grip of pure panic, but in her memory, it felt like an assault. These fragments play in her mind not as a narrative she can process, but like a film that plays over and over, each viewing as raw as the first. Because these sensory fragments are so dominated by sound and touch, her mind has become intensely attuned to any sudden noise or unexpected physical contact, treating them as imminent warnings.

The sensory echoes of that moment now dictate her life. Because the memories can surface without warning, triggered by the most mundane events, she has come to believe she is never truly safe. This conviction has hollowed out her sleep; she lies awake for hours, certain she must stay alert, her body rigid and her ears straining for any sound. Even in the quiet of her own home, she is unable to relax, constantly scanning rooms for threats she cannot name. The memories feed this pervasive sense of threat; when a fragment of the explosion surfaces, her body responds as if it is happening now, her heart pounding as she scans her surroundings for danger. She feels profound shame when these memories come, a burning sense of failure for having frozen, for not having done more to help the others in the van, for having survived when others did not. This shame reinforces her belief that she is helpless, that she is fundamentally unable to stop bad things from happening.

At her veterinary clinic, a place that was once her sanctuary, the world is now a minefield of triggers. A dropped metal water bowl, a loud noise that once would have been an annoyance, now brings the memory of the explosion rushing back with visceral force. When a colleague places an unexpected hand on her shoulder to get her attention, the tactile shock sends a jolt of panic through her, and for a second, she is back in the dark, chaotic van. These triggers not only bring back the memory but also confirm her most deep-seated fears about the world and herself; each startling sound or touch is fresh evidence that she can't rely on herself to stay safe. Driving, once a simple act, has become an ordeal. She can no longer be a passenger, as the feeling of being in a vehicle with others is inextricably linked to the trauma.

Her negative appraisals have become the lens through which she views everything. The profound sense that what happened to her was deeply unfair, and that no one has been held accountable, keeps the memory raw and immediate, preventing it from settling into the past. It is this feeling of injustice that seems to demand the memory replay itself, as if her mind is refusing to let the event go until some cosmic balance is restored. This belief in her own helplessness has, in turn, made her hypervigilant to the very triggers that torment her; because she is certain she cannot protect herself, she is always listening for the next loud noise or anticipating the next unexpected touch, which only makes her more susceptible to being startled by them.

The cycles have tightened over the months, creating a feedback loop of fear and avoidance. The intrusive memories, steeped in shame, reinforce her conviction that she is broken and helpless. The constant state of threat and hypervigilance has exhausted her, which she interprets as further proof that she can’t rely on herself. Her husband’s attempts to comfort her, to touch her, are now another source of threat. She has started taking separate cars to family events, a change that has created a painful distance in her marriage. Kealani sought therapy after her husband told her, his voice heavy with sadness, that he felt he was living with a ghost. Her greatest fear is that he is right, and that the vibrant, confident woman she once was is gone for good. Her hope is a simple, yet seemingly impossible one: to one day feel safe in her own skin again.
